countryDocs.title: Legal requirements for AI assisted exam grading in the United States
countryDocs.filename: AI Exam Grading - Legal and Regulatory Requirements - US.docx

intro.text: Legal requirements for AI assisted exam grading in the United States

Classification: National Law means federal legislation; State Law and District Law identify subnational statutes, not municipal Local Law. Regulations are identified separately from their parent statutes. Contractual terms are not statutes and bind only where actually agreed. This updates the supplied federal and selected-state research; it is not a complete survey of all 50 states or every district policy.

sections.title: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act

blocks.text: Instrument type: National Law — federal; Regulation — federal implementing rules (separate matrix columns).

Institution receiving applicable federal education funding: Treat identifiable scripts, marks, feedback and other records maintained by or for the institution as education records. Before disclosing them to a vendor, obtain signed and dated consent identifying the records, purpose and recipients, or satisfy a specific FERPA exception. Rights normally belong to the parent until the student turns 18 or attends a postsecondary institution.

Institution using the school-official exception: The vendor must perform an institutional function for which employees would otherwise be used, remain under the institution’s direct control over the use and maintenance of records, and comply with § 99.33 use and redisclosure limits. The institution’s annual notice must define school officials and legitimate educational interests. Use reasonable methods to restrict access to records needed for those interests. A teacher’s account registration alone does not establish these conditions; a teacher may act only within actual institutional authority.

Provider: Use records only for the purpose for which disclosure was made. Do not use identifiable scripts for independent model training, advertising or other customers unless a separate lawful disclosure and use route permits it. Ensure any further recipient is covered by a lawful redisclosure arrangement. FERPA itself does not universally require a written school-official contract, but state law frequently does and the institution must be able to demonstrate direct control.

Institution and provider: Enable inspection and review within 45 days and the statutory process for challenging inaccurate, misleading or privacy-infringing records. This record-correction process does not require changing a correctly recorded academic judgment merely because the student disputes it. Preserve required disclosure records, subject to the exceptions in § 99.32.

Institution using de-identified data – 34 CFR § 99.31(b)(1): Remove direct and indirect identifiers and make a reasonable determination that the student is not identifiable from the release, multiple releases and other reasonably available information. Removing names alone does not establish de-identification. The institution or other authorised releasing party must make that determination. This disclosure route removes the relevant FERPA consent requirement; it does not give a teacher independent authority to extract or release institutional records for a free product-development trial. Obtain any institutional authority required for preparing and releasing the material; existing authority can cover it.

Institution using the studies exception: Limit the study to a permitted purpose, such as improving instruction. Sign the required agreement specifying purpose, scope, duration and disclosed information; restrict identifiable access to representatives with legitimate interests, prohibit unrelated use and specify when identifiable data will be destroyed. Calling a commercial pilot a study does not by itself meet the exception.

sections.title: Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act and Rule

blocks.text: Instrument type: National Law — federal; Regulation — federal implementing rules (separate matrix columns).
15 USC §§ 6501–6506; 16 CFR Part 312, as amended in 2025

links.label: 15 USC §§ 6501–6506; 16 CFR Part 312, as amended in 2025

blocks.text: FTC guidance on school authorisation

Covered online operator: Where a child-directed service, or a service with actual knowledge, collects personal information online from children under 13, provide the required online and direct notices and obtain verifiable parental consent before collection, use or disclosure unless a specific exception applies. A teacher uploading a pupil’s script to a service used only by adults does not automatically satisfy this child-collection trigger.

Provider relying on school authorisation under FTC guidance: Limit collection and use to the school-authorised educational purpose for the school’s benefit. Give the school the required information and access, deletion and collection-stopping controls. School authorisation cannot cover unrelated commercial use. Obtain parental consent where required for those uses; do not shift the operator’s compliance responsibility to teachers.

Provider: Under the amended Rule, obtain separate parental consent for covered third-party disclosures unless disclosure is integral to the service. Do not require more information than reasonably necessary. Maintain a written information-security programme, assess and address risks, review it at least annually, and obtain appropriate security assurances from service providers. Maintain a written retention policy specifying purposes, retention periods and deletion timetable; do not retain children’s information indefinitely. Provide parental access, deletion and prevention of further collection. The general compliance deadline for the 2025 amendments was 22 April 2026.
Instrument type: National Law — federal.

Covered institution: Before requiring an applicable federally funded survey, analysis or evaluation revealing protected information, obtain the required written parental consent or eligible-student consent. Protected topics include political beliefs, mental or psychological problems, sexual behaviour or attitudes, illegal or self-incriminating behaviour, critical appraisals of close family, privileged relationships, religious beliefs and specified income information.

Institution: For other covered protected-information surveys and marketing-data activities, adopt the required policies, give notices and provide inspection or opt-out rights as applicable. Ordinary rubric-based academic marking is not automatically a protected-topic survey; do not add sensitive inference or profiling activities without reassessing this trigger.

sections.title: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act

blocks.text: Instrument type: National Law — federal.

Institution receiving federal financial assistance: Do not exclude, deny benefits to, or discriminate against students on grounds of race, colour or national origin. Ensure use of AI does not implement unlawful discrimination in assessment. Correct discriminatory practices and do not knowingly adopt discriminatory scoring rules merely because a vendor generated them.

sections.title: Title IX of the Education Amendments

blocks.text: Instrument type: National Law — federal.

Covered federally funded education programme: Do not discriminate on the basis of sex, subject to statutory exceptions. Apply lawful assessment criteria and investigate and correct unlawful differential treatment in AI-assisted assessment. Vendor use does not transfer the institution’s obligations.
Instrument type: National Law — federal; Regulation — federal implementing rules (separate matrix columns).

Covered institution and teacher: Implement required disability accommodations and evaluate the student’s relevant attainment rather than the effect of an impairment unrelated to that attainment. Do not let handwriting recognition, inaccessible interfaces or automated scoring negate approved accommodations. For placement or special-education evaluation, use the required information and qualified decision-makers; a single AI score cannot replace the prescribed evaluation process.
Instrument type: National Law — federal; Regulation — federal implementing rules (separate matrix columns).

Covered school and teacher: Deliver the assessment accommodations in the student’s IEP. When conducting an IDEA evaluation, use a variety of assessment tools and strategies, do not use a single measure as the sole eligibility criterion, and use technically sound, nondiscriminatory instruments administered by trained personnel. Ordinary classroom grading and an IDEA eligibility evaluation must not be conflated.
Instrument type: National Law — federal; Regulation — federal implementing rules (separate matrix columns).
42 USC §§ 12132 and 12182; 28 CFR Part 35, including Subpart H

links.label: 42 USC §§ 12132 and 12182; 28 CFR Part 35, including Subpart H

blocks.text: Covered public institution: Provide effective communication, reasonable modifications and equal access. For covered web content and mobile apps, including services supplied through a vendor arrangement, meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA by the applicable deadline, subject to the rule’s specific exceptions. Following the 2026 extension, the dates are 26 April 2027 for public entities with populations of at least 50,000 and 26 April 2028 for smaller entities and special district governments. School districts use the rule’s school-district population method; they are not automatically special district governments.

Covered private educational institution: Meet the applicable Title III nondiscrimination, reasonable-modification and auxiliary-aid duties. The Title II technical rule and its deadlines do not automatically apply to every private school or every vendor.
Instrument type: Regulation — federal.
34 CFR § 600.2, definition of distance education

Title IV participating higher-education institution: For a course treated as distance education, ensure regular and substantive interaction with qualified instructors as defined by the regulation. Where assessing or giving feedback is used to satisfy the substantive-interaction requirement, provide the required instructor interaction. Automated feedback alone does not substitute for interaction with an instructor.
Instrument type: National Law — federal.

Provider within FTC jurisdiction: Do not make materially misleading claims about grading accuracy, bias, privacy, human review, security or legal approval. Hold adequate evidence for objective performance claims before making them. Honour privacy and retention commitments and avoid unfair practices that cause substantial, unavoidable injury not outweighed by countervailing benefits. Do not describe a system as regulator-approved without the actual approval claimed.
Instrument type: National Law — federal.

Provider and institution, where protected content is copied: Ensure that uploading, storing or otherwise reproducing protected student work, examination questions or third-party mark schemes is covered by the necessary rights or an applicable exception. Copyright does not require a separate approval merely to make an academic judgment. Existing rights can suffice; fresh permission for every script is not automatically required. Where relying on fair use, evaluate its statutory factors for the actual copying and purpose; educational use is not an automatic exemption. Permission to process work for an institution’s assessment does not automatically authorise independent model training or other reuse.
Instrument type: State Law.
Education Law § 2-d

Educational agency and third-party contractor receiving covered data: Include the required privacy protections and Parents’ Bill of Rights in the contract, together with the supplementary information on purposes, subcontractors, duration, data disposition, accuracy challenges, storage and security. Limit use to the contracted educational purpose. Do not sell or disclose personally identifiable information for commercial purposes; restrict employee access to what is necessary and protect confidentiality.
Instrument type: Regulation — state.
8 NYCRR Part 121, especially §§ 121.3 and 121.6–7

Provider: Include an agency-accepted data security and privacy plan in each covered contract. Specify safeguards, trained personnel, subcontractor controls, incident handling and deletion or return. Comply with the agency’s policy and the applicable NIST Cybersecurity Framework requirements. Report a breach or unauthorised release to the agency without unreasonable delay and no later than seven calendar days after discovery; meet the applicable notification-cost obligations.

Agency: Publish required contract information and maintain its own data security and privacy policy, separate from the contractor’s plan. Make the required breach notifications and provide the statutory complaint route.
Instrument type: State Law.
Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 10-234aa–10-234dd

Contractor and local or regional board: Before covered processing, include the mandatory contract terms: data ownership by the student or board, authorised purposes, access and correction rights, protection measures, disclosure and sale restrictions, breach notice, deletion or return, legal compliance, Connecticut governing law and the contractual consequences specified by the statute. Do not claim ownership of student records or use them beyond the authorised educational purpose.

Board: Publish the contract on its website within five business days after execution. Provider: Meet the applicable incident-notification rules in § 10-234dd; for a breach involving student information, notify the board without unreasonable delay and within the statutory 30-day outer limit. Do not rely on the board’s publication duties to satisfy the provider’s own duties.

sections.title: Illinois Student Online Personal Protection Act

blocks.text: Instrument type: State Law.
105 ILCS 85, especially §§ 10, 15 and 27

Covered operator: Do not engage in prohibited targeted advertising, non-school-purpose profiling, sale or unauthorised disclosure of covered information. Maintain reasonable security meeting or exceeding industry standards, publish material data practices and delete covered school-controlled information within a reasonable period on request, subject to the statutory exception.

Operator and public school: Execute the required written agreement, identifying data and services, the school-official role, breach costs and deletion or transfer arrangements. Publish or make the agreement available as required, with only permitted redactions. Notify the school of a breach as expediently as possible without unreasonable delay and no later than 30 calendar days after determining a breach occurred. Provide the recipient list at least at the beginning of each state fiscal year and each calendar year.

sections.title: Colorado Student Data Transparency and Security Act

blocks.text: Instrument type: State Law.

Covered school service provider: Publish understandable information on collected student data, uses and sharing. Use data only for authorised school purposes; do not sell data, use it for targeted advertising or create unauthorised profiles. Maintain the required security programme, support correction of inaccurate information, control subcontractors and meet deletion obligations. Notify the contracting education provider of material policy changes and unauthorised disclosure as required; the notice obligation is not confined to incidents the vendor considers serious.
Education provider: Apply the statutory contract, transparency and security requirements and ensure the agreed destruction or return process operates when the contract ends.

sections.title: California Student Online Personal Information Protection Act

blocks.text: Instrument type: State Law.
California Business and Professions Code § 22584

qa.title: What does the GDPR require for AI assisted grading?

blocks.text: Processing identifiable scripts requires a lawful basis for processing and external disclosure, controlled recipients, suitable security, limited retention, transparent information and workable student rights. Where the vendor is a processor, binding processing terms and subprocessor controls are required. Special-category data needs an additional legal condition. A DPIA is required where processing is likely to create high risk. Removing names does not necessarily anonymise a script. In Germany, solely automated significant decisions are restricted by Article 22. The UK has its own amended Articles 22A–22D: ordinary-data automation can be lawful with safeguards, while special-category decisions remain restricted. FERPA and applicable US laws govern the US context.
EU GDPR
UK Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 80

links.label: UK Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 80

qa.title: What does the EU AI Act require?

blocks.text: An AI system intended to evaluate learning outcomes is generally within Annex III point 3(b). Human final marking alone does not remove that classification. Where high-risk duties apply, the provider needs risk and quality management, suitable data and testing, technical documentation, logs, human-oversight capabilities and the required conformity and registration steps. Institutions have separate deployment and impact-assessment duties. The amended start date for Chapter III Sections 1–3 for Annex III systems is 2 December 2027. AI-literacy measures and applicable prohibited-practice and transparency rules already apply. The amendment does not expressly defer Section 5; do not treat the date change as a blanket suspension of market-access requirements.

qa.title: Which requirements apply below the EU level in Germany?

blocks.text: The relevant Land’s school or higher-education law, school-data rules, examination regulations, service rules and staff-participation requirements apply. The responsible examiner must retain the assessment required by examination law, follow consistent criteria and support review of challenged marks. A KMK recommendation coordinates policy but does not itself approve a vendor or override a Land’s rules. Supervisory guidance explains the authorities’ position; distinguish it from binding legislation and applicable official instructions.

qa.title: Why does AI matter compared with ordinary data processing?

blocks.text: Privacy law already covers ordinary digital processing of identifiable scripts. AI adds inferred scores and judgments, error and bias risks, possible profiling, and potentially significant automated decisions. Those features can trigger additional assessments, safeguards and AI-specific duties. The legal trigger is the system’s actual purpose and effects; using a human reviewer does not erase every AI or privacy obligation.
AI Act, Articles 3 and 6

qa.title: Can a teacher use the service independently or must the institution authorise it?

blocks.text: A teacher can use it within the authority and arrangements granted by the responsible institution. A personal subscription does not authorise external disclosure of student data. In Germany and the UK, the relevant controller must establish lawful processing, contracts and required assessments; a teacher may carry out delegated tasks. In the US, the institution must satisfy FERPA’s disclosure conditions and applicable state and district rules. Separate qualification or examination restrictions may apply even to an institution-approved tool.
FERPA
UK GDPR, Articles 28 and 29

qa.title: Could one national or regional decision authorise all schools and teachers?

blocks.text: There is no universal approval that displaces the underlying duties. In Germany, a Land can act within its educational powers, while the Bund cannot simply approve a service for every Land’s schools. A regional instruction or contract must still respect data protection, examination law and institutional responsibilities. In the US, state or district arrangements can support wider adoption without removing FERPA and local requirements. In the UK, authority depends on the nation, institution and procurement structure; a national platform listing alone does not approve every assessment use.
Basic Law, Articles 30 and 70
FERPA

qa.title: May a provider offer AI grading solely for comparison or validation of a teacher’s own evaluation as a second opinion (“Zweitmeinung”)?

blocks.text: A provider may offer a compliant comparison product, subject to the applicable market-access rules. That does not authorise every school to use it. A second opinion requires a lawful data flow and the applicable institutional and assessment authority. Bremen’s 2026 guidance permits supporting recommendations under teacher responsibility without personal-data transmission and with advance transparency. Schleswig-Holstein’s published guide rejects AI assessment of pupil work; Baden-Württemberg’s authority distinguishes learning support from impermissible grade-equivalent assessment. A final teacher signature does not cure a prohibited workflow.

Sources: the Germany document, section 20, records the official guidance for all 16 states and its date, scope and legal status. The Länder material concerns schools; university assessment regulations require a separate institution-specific check.

Germany and the EU AI Act: Article 6(3)(c) and recital 53 expressly contemplate checking a teacher’s completed grading pattern for inconsistencies. This can support the exception from high-risk classification if the exact conditions are met. The provider must establish the absence of significant risk, the qualifying limited purpose and the absence of profiling of natural persons, and document the assessment and meet the applicable registration duty. A system that independently scores identifiable students may still perform profiling and remain high-risk. Calling it a second opinion is insufficient. A comparison intended to alter the final mark also requires assessment of its actual influence. It cannot replace a legally required second human examiner.

UK: Teacher-led comparison or quality assurance can be permissible. For Ofqual-regulated qualifications, the awarding organisation must preserve the required human marking and its assessment rules. A genuinely retrospective comparison without significant effects is different from a solely automated significant decision, but UK GDPR still governs the data.

US: Such a service can be offered, with FERPA and applicable state and district conditions met. State AI rules depend on actual use: Oklahoma preserves educator review and bars AI as the primary basis of grading, while Colorado’s 2027 duties target material influence on consequential decisions. A comparison-only label does not defeat those triggers if practice differs.

qa.title: Is the student’s consent required?

blocks.text: Not automatically. The answer depends on the legal basis, the data and the intended use, including comparison-only use.

Germany and UK: Consent is unnecessary where another valid legal basis covers both the assessment and the external processing, such as a legally supported public task. The institution must establish that basis before uploading scripts; educational usefulness alone is insufficient. If relying on consent, it must be informed, specific, freely given and withdrawable, with a real alternative and no unfair disadvantage for refusal. For minors, determine whether the student or a parent or guardian can validly consent. Special-category data and significant automated decisions require the additional conditions or safeguards explained in Question 1.

US: FERPA generally requires signed, dated consent for disclosure unless an exception applies. A properly established school-official arrangement can permit disclosure without consent. FERPA consent rights belong to the parent until they transfer to the eligible student at 18 or on attendance at a postsecondary institution. If COPPA applies to online collection from under-13s, the operator generally needs parental consent; qualifying school authorisation can cover solely educational use under FTC guidance. Applicable state laws may impose additional consent or opt-out requirements.

qa.title: Is consent from the school or university required in every case?

blocks.text: For official use, the teacher needs the required institutional authority; a separate consent for every use is unnecessary. Existing approval, an approved contract or delegated authority can cover the service and purpose. The competent body may be the school, university, district, trust or education authority, depending on local arrangements.

In Germany and the UK, this concerns the responsible controller’s authorisation, processor terms and instructions, rather than the institution giving student-style GDPR consent. In the US, the relevant institution must satisfy FERPA and applicable state and district conditions; the school-official exception requires institutional control over the vendor’s use of records. Student consent does not by itself authorise a teacher to disregard institutional or examination rules.

Offering the product, or privately testing it with self-created examples, does not universally require school permission. Use of genuinely anonymised material may avoid student-data consent requirements, but anonymising real scripts must itself be lawful, and confidentiality, copyright, employment and examination rules can still require approval. The same limits apply to a second opinion.

qa.title: Can a teacher use the tool without school or university permission, for example for experimental testing, information or comparison, or under other conditions?

blocks.text: Yes, in limited circumstances. Here, school “consent” means institutional authorisation. The purpose and data used matter; calling a use experimental, informational or comparison-only does not itself create an exemption.

Private exploration can need no school permission. A teacher can, for example, try a provider’s demonstration or compare their own invented answers with AI feedback using synthetic examples or lawfully reusable public material containing no student or other third-party personal data. This assumes no confidential school material is used, no commitment is made on the institution’s behalf, and no applicable employment, IT, copyright or other rule requires approval. A private account does not make official school work private.

A separate request may be unnecessary within existing authority. General research or lesson preparation with non-personal material may fall within the teacher’s professional discretion where applicable rules permit that choice. An approved tool, central contract or delegated authority may also already cover the specific testing or comparison. The teacher must stay within that scope; authority to teach or mark does not automatically authorise a new external data recipient or contract.

Real student work remains subject to the rules even if no grade changes. Uploading identifiable scripts for a pilot, validation or a second opinion still processes school data. Germany and UK require the relevant controller’s authority and lawful processing arrangements; in the US, applicable FERPA disclosure conditions and state and institutional rules still apply. Student consent does not override required institutional authority. Research is not a general permission to bypass these requirements.

Anonymisation or offline use can remove particular obligations, but not all approval requirements. Genuinely anonymous inputs can fall outside personal-data rules; removing names alone is insufficient. Accessing and anonymising original school records must itself be lawful and authorised. A fully local tool that sends no data to the supplier avoids that external disclosure, but school processing and IT rules remain. Neither condition overrides confidentiality, copyright, examination rules or an applicable institutional approval policy.
EU GDPR, recital 26 and Articles 5–6, 28–29

qa.title: If real submissions are genuinely anonymised before upload, does a teacher still need school approval for a free, non-production product test or development trial?

blocks.text: A new approval can be unnecessary, but true anonymisation alone does not remove every approval requirement. Assuming the scrambling achieves genuine anonymisation, the teacher can conduct the trial without an additional school approval if existing authority already permits preparing and reusing that material and no applicable rule requires separate approval for the trial.

The anonymity standard is contextual, not a fixed probability percentage. Identification must not be reasonably likely using available means, considering other information, time, cost and technology. The assessment includes matching against original scripts, retained links and metadata. The answer below assumes that the relevant legal standard is actually met before the provider receives the trial material.

Germany and UK: the subsequent anonymous-data trial falls outside GDPR for those inputs. Processing genuinely anonymous submissions does not itself require a GDPR lawful basis, student consent or an Article 28 DPA for those submissions. GDPR does not impose a separate school-approval requirement for that anonymous processing. Personal data used elsewhere in the service, such as account details, must be assessed separately.

The earlier anonymisation step remains regulated. Accessing, copying and scrambling identifiable school records is personal-data processing. It needs a lawful basis and must stay within the responsible controller’s instructions. Existing instructions or delegated authority can cover this; a new signature is not automatically necessary. However, permission to mark scripts does not automatically include extracting and anonymising them for an external product-development trial. If that activity is outside the teacher’s authority, approval is still needed before that step. Later anonymity does not cure an unauthorised use of the originals.

US: FERPA permits properly de-identified disclosure without student or parental consent. Under 34 CFR 99.31(b)(1), the institution or other authorised releasing party must reasonably determine that identification is not possible from the release, multiple releases and other reasonably available information. This removes the relevant FERPA consent requirement; it does not independently grant a teacher authority to release institutional records.

Other approval rules can still apply. Confidentiality, copyright, employment duties, school or university IT policies and rules for external research or product trials may require permission even for anonymous material. Free access and trial-only use do not override them. If preparation and reuse are already lawfully permitted and none of these rules requires a further decision, the teacher need not obtain a new school approval solely because the trial uses AI.

qa.title: Do university professors need university approval to use an AI exam grading service, or may they choose the software independently?

blocks.text: A separate approval is not automatically required for every software choice, but professorial status is not a general exemption. A professor may choose tools within the applicable university rules and their actual authority. Discretion over teaching or marking does not automatically authorise external disclosure of student work or acceptance of contracts on the university’s behalf.

Germany and UK: Where the university is the controller, the service must fit its lawful processing arrangements, documented instructions and required processor terms. Existing approval, a central agreement or delegated authority may cover the professor’s use. If the proposed service or purpose falls outside that authority, the professor must obtain the required institutional decision before uploading identifiable scripts. University examination rules also continue to govern the professor’s own assessment responsibility.

US: A FERPA-covered university must meet the applicable disclosure conditions. Under the school-official exception, the vendor must perform the qualifying institutional function and remain under the university’s direct control over use and maintenance of records. A professor’s personal registration alone does not establish this. Applicable state law and university contracting, IT and assessment rules may impose further requirements.

Independent use can be permissible where university rules allow that choice and existing arrangements cover the actual data, provider and purpose. Private testing with self-created examples, or a lawfully authorised trial using genuinely anonymous material, can avoid particular student-data requirements; confidentiality, copyright and applicable institutional rules still matter. See Questions 9a and 9b. A personal account or payment from the professor’s own funds does not itself remove these obligations.

Apply higher-education rules to the actual institution. A school-specific approval rule or a K–12 statute does not automatically apply to universities. In England, OfS condition B4 governs assessment at registered higher-education providers; Ofqual’s rules apply within the scope of its regulated qualifications. Neither professorial discretion nor an institution-approved tool permits disregarding applicable examination requirements.
EU GDPR, Articles 5–6, 24 and 28–29
UK GDPR, Articles 5–6, 24 and 28–29

qa.title: Once the service meets legal and regulatory requirements, can the school headmaster or university decide to use it, or are other approvals required?

blocks.text: Yes, if the decision falls within its authority and all requirements for the actual deployment have been met. The existing documents identify no universal additional ministry or regulator approval merely because grading assistance uses AI. However, confirming the provider’s compliance does not establish that the institution has completed its own required decisions and procedures.

Germany-specific qualification: Bavaria’s 28 November 2025 guidance expressly calls for school-head release before AI is used as a school operating tool. Lower Saxony’s school rules also contain an approval requirement for the relevant digital systems. Existing approval may suffice, but an anonymous input alone does not override a tool-approval rule. The NRW, Baden-Württemberg and Schleswig-Holstein assessment restrictions require their own analysis; they cannot be satisfied solely by teacher acceptance of vendor terms.

The authorised decision-maker matters. A headmaster may decide within delegated powers; a school board, district, trust, education authority or other responsible body may hold the relevant authority instead. A university must follow its own allocation of contracting, IT and examination powers. Existing institutional approval or a central agreement can already cover the proposed use. Any applicable purchasing procedure concerns acquiring the service; it is not a general permission requirement for marking with software.

Germany: Applicable Land and examination rules still govern who may approve the use and how assessment is conducted. A headmaster or university cannot waive a prescribed examiner or marking procedure. Required staff participation must also be completed: for example, § 72 LPVG NRW for covered technical monitoring of employees, or § 87(1) no. 6 BetrVG for covered private employers. These requirements depend on their scope and the system’s functions; they do not apply to every AI tool automatically.

UK: For regulated qualifications, obtain any permission required by the awarding organisation’s assessment arrangements. Institutional approval alone cannot change those arrangements or permit sole AI marking of Ofqual-regulated assessments in England. University use must also remain within applicable examination rules; OfS condition B4 applies to registered higher-education providers in England.

US: Follow applicable state and district assessment policies and institutional contracting authority. For FERPA-covered records disclosed under the school-official exception, the institution must retain the required direct control over the vendor. A principal’s decision cannot replace a board or other institutional decision where the applicable arrangements reserve that authority.

Regulator consultation is exceptional, not routine. Under EU and UK GDPR Articles 35–36, consult the supervisory authority before processing where a required data-protection impact assessment leaves a high risk that cannot be adequately mitigated. If the competent institution has completed all triggered approvals and procedures, the materials identify no further general AI-use approval to obtain.

qa.title: What risks do regulators see if students can challenge every assessment item and the teacher then makes a final judgment without relying on AI?

blocks.text: An effective appeal reduces risk but does not eliminate it. Regulators are concerned about inaccurate or discriminatory grades, unreliable explanations and excessive reliance on suggested scores, because results affect educational and career opportunities. Data security and confidentiality risks also arise before any appeal.

Applied to the described workflow: If teachers review only challenged items, errors in unchallenged marks can remain. Students may not recognise an error or be equally able to contest it; teachers may be influenced by the initial suggestion. If every effective grade instead reflects the teacher’s substantive judgment before it has significant consequences, the decision can be human. A later appeal does not retrospectively make an earlier solely automated significant decision human; Germany and the UK apply different automation rules, as explained in Question 1.

Under the EU AI Act, evaluating learning outcomes generally falls within Annex III even with an appeal route. A limited comparison use may qualify for Article 6(3), subject to its conditions; see Question 7. If AI truly never affects the grade, the grading risk is substantially reduced, but privacy, security and applicable examination duties remain.

qa.title: How does the law treat ordinary IT supported grading differently from AI supported grading, and how much does the AI designation matter?

blocks.text: The basic duties apply to both. Privacy, confidentiality, security, non-discrimination and examination rules do not depend on an AI label. Significant automated-decision rules are technology-neutral: fixed-rule software can trigger them, while AI assistance with meaningful human decision-making may not be solely automated.

Germany and the EU: The AI Act adds duties where the system meets its functional AI definition and the relevant risk classification. Simple arithmetic or a fixed human-written answer key generally falls outside that definition. A model that infers a score or assessment can fall inside it. Predictable outputs or calling the product ordinary IT do not settle the classification. The additional high-risk requirements and timing are in Question 2.

UK and US: Do not automatically import EU classifications into domestic law. In England, Ofqual applies its existing assessment framework to AI, including its restriction on sole AI marking in regulated qualifications. US FERPA applies regardless of technology; state AI and automated-decision laws have their own definitions and triggers. The system’s functions, influence and jurisdiction determine which additional rules apply.

qa.title: Do any of the applicable norms prohibit submitting data to AI, as distinct from data processing in general?

blocks.text: There is no general GDPR prohibition on every AI upload or every non-EU provider. However, several official German school guides expressly rule out pupil personal data in the AI use cases they describe, and some assessment rules or interpretations are stricter than a human-sign-off model. The answer must therefore distinguish general data-protection law, the particular Land’s guidance or instructions, examination rules and the actual tool configuration.

Under EU and UK data-protection law, a particular upload can be unlawful because it lacks a legal basis, exceeds authorised instructions, exposes data to uncontrolled recipients, or involves an unlawful international transfer. Allowing a provider to reuse scripts for its own model training requires a separate legal assessment. FERPA similarly restricts disclosure and reuse of identifiable education records; an AI service receives no special exemption.

Specific restrictions still apply. For example, Ofqual does not permit AI as the sole marker in assessments forming part of regulated qualifications in England. That restricts the assessment use, rather than every transfer of data to AI. Institutional rules may also prohibit uploading confidential scripts to unapproved services.

An approved service can therefore be permissible where the same data sent to a public AI service is not. Truly anonymous data can fall outside personal-data rules, but confidentiality, copyright and applicable AI or examination rules can still apply.

The Germany supplement distinguishes these positions across all 16 states. For example, Bremen describes supported assessment without personal-data transmission; Bavaria requires prior release and controlled contractual/data arrangements; Schleswig-Holstein’s 2023 guide rejects AI assessment of pupil work. A platform’s EU hosting or no-training statement is not proof that the same configuration exists in Gradias. Guidance is labelled as guidance and is not automatically a new statutory prohibition.

qa.title: Is hiding the student’s identity sufficient evidence that AI grading is free from bias?

blocks.text: No. Removing names can reduce identity-based influence, but does not prove freedom from bias. A model can produce unequal errors from linguistic style, cultural references or handwriting recognition without knowing who wrote the answer. Other features can act as proxies for protected characteristics. Whether a penalty is justified also depends on the subject and rubric: spelling can legitimately matter in some assessments and be irrelevant in others.

Anonymisation and fairness answer different questions. Masking a name is not necessarily anonymisation. A school’s workflow remains personal-data processing where it can reconnect scripts and students; identifiability in the provider’s hands requires its own contextual assessment. Even genuinely anonymous inputs do not establish fair grading.

Appropriate evidence should include validation against independently reviewed human reference grades, representative scripts, rubric-level error analysis and tests for unjustified disparities across relevant groups where lawful. Test handwriting recognition where used, record limitations and corrections, and reassess after material changes. These are practical ways to evidence reliability and bias controls, not a universal statutory test or a guarantee of zero bias.

Audit data about protected characteristics needs its own lawful basis and any required special-category condition. It can be held separately from operational marking inputs; the grading model need not receive student identities to test fairness.

qa.title: Must the provider conclude a DPA with the school, and can standard provider terms be accepted simply through registration or use?

blocks.text: Germany and UK: normally yes where the provider processes personal data on the institution’s behalf. Article 28 requires binding written processing terms, including electronic form, or another qualifying legal act, before processing starts. The controller may be the school, university, district or responsible authority. A separate paper document or handwritten signature is not universally required. If the provider acts as an independent controller for a purpose, a processor DPA does not resolve that processing.

Standard provider terms can work if they form an enforceable agreement and include all Article 28 requirements. They must specify the processing, duration, data and people concerned, controller rights, instructions, confidentiality, security, subprocessors, assistance with rights and compliance, deletion or return, audit rights and notification of unlawful instructions. A privacy policy alone is insufficient; terms must accurately cover the actual service.

Registration can conclude the DPA if an authorised institutional representative validly accepts clearly incorporated terms and applicable contract and public-sector requirements are met. A practical implementation is an explicit acceptance of the linked DPA before uploads, recording the institution, authorised person, date and agreed version, with a downloadable copy. This is a way to evidence agreement, not a universally prescribed checkbox format. Mere use or an unauthorised teacher’s personal registration does not automatically bind the institution. A central agreement can already cover authorised users; individual teachers need not each sign again.

US: FERPA’s school-official exception does not itself universally require a written DPA, but institutional control over use and disclosure remains necessary. Other FERPA exceptions and state laws can require written agreements. Click acceptance must satisfy those requirements and institutional contracting rules; registration alone does not establish compliance.

qa.title: Under GDPR, must the provider have DPAs with subprocessors, especially LLM providers?

blocks.text: Yes, where the provider acts as the school’s processor and the LLM provider processes personal data on its behalf. Article 28(4) and (9) require binding written processing terms, including electronic form, or another qualifying legal act, before subprocessing starts. This also applies to other subcontractors processing the school’s personal data.

The provider must obtain the controller’s prior specific or general written authorisation. With general authorisation, it must notify intended additions or replacements and give the controller an opportunity to object. The subprocessor agreement must impose the same data-protection obligations as the school’s DPA, adapted to the outsourced activity: instructions, confidentiality, security, breach and rights assistance, deletion or return, audit access and controls over further subprocessors. The provider remains fully liable to the controller for its subprocessor’s performance of those obligations.

An LLM provider’s standard DPA can suffice if it is binding, covers the actual service and meets these requirements; it need not repeat the school DPA word for word. See Question 14 on electronic acceptance. The school generally contracts with the grading provider, which contracts with its subprocessor; the school need not separately sign every downstream DPA. Where an intermediary supplies the LLM service, the required agreements and authorisations must extend through the processing chain. International transfers must separately satisfy GDPR Chapter V.

For LLMs, a no-training setting does not replace a DPA: inference still processes personal data. Own-purpose model training can make the LLM provider a controller for that activity and needs a separate legal assessment. A locally run model with no vendor processing of personal data does not itself create a subprocessing relationship. Removing student names alone does not establish anonymisation; see Question 13.

qa.title: Do all German states have the same published AI grading rules?

blocks.text: No. Official material was found for every Land, but it differs in legal status, age and subject. Some guides address pupils using AI to write work, others address teacher assistance; those are different questions. Saarland’s verified material is platform-specific AIS.chat guidance. Sachsen-Anhalt’s official publication notice confirms a guide to complex student work, but the linked full text was not reliably accessible during this review; no detailed obligations were inferred from the unavailable text. The Germany document lists all 16 states, the specific sources and the limits of each finding.

A KMK recommendation is not a federal statute and does not supersede a Land’s school law or an institution’s assessment rules. Existing NRW sources have all been included: the Ministry’s 2023 guide, the Medienberatung FAQ and the LDI’s 2026 annual report. Their different scope explains why a cautious FAQ statement about personal data must not be converted into a blanket interpretation of every legally controlled school AI deployment.

qa.title: How should the requirement matrix be read?

blocks.text: Rows are actual requirements derived from the research; the original sample rows have been replaced. Each column identifies an instrument, its type, scope and effective-date status. Yes means the requirement is stated in the reviewed relevant provisions or guidance, subject to the cell note. No means it is not stated there; it is not legal permission and does not override another instrument. An impact assessment, consent, institutional approval and a processing contract have different triggers. Recommendations, regulatory conditions and contract-dependent standards are labelled separately from legislation. Generic unsigned contracts are not treated as verified law.

qa.title: Which earlier Gradias claims need correction before reuse?

blocks.text: The older Website/General Terms compliance drafts contain broad claims about independent teacher use, no school DPA, the provider always being a controller and human final review removing high-risk classification. Those claims should not be reused as legal conclusions. The correct answer depends on actual roles, institutional authority, Article 28 or local contract duties, the assessment function and the applicable state or qualification rules. No source establishes a general exemption for a free trial using real student records.

Statements about actual EU-only processing, absence of training, subprocessors, deletion, certificates, completed DPIAs or technical compliance need operational evidence. The legal research identifies requirements; it does not certify the product. The older drafts and archives are retained as historical inputs, with conflicts identified in the source register. Drata and Vanta links are vendor references, not evidence of a certification or legal requirement.

states.name: Baden-Württemberg
states.instrument: LfDI: Rechtsgrundlagen Datenschutz und KI | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Die Aufsicht unterscheidet technische Lernunterstützung nach § 115b Abs. 9 SchG von benotungsäquivalenter Leistungsbeurteilung; Letztere ist nach ihrer Auslegung unzulässig. Die allgemeinen schulischen Grundlagen tragen kein beliebiges Training mit Schülerdaten. Diese aufsichtsbehördliche Rechtsauslegung ist keine neue Verordnung; eine Freigabe durch die Lehrkraft ersetzt die erforderliche gesetzliche Grundlage nicht.
states.limits: Veraltete KI-VO-Fristen im Webtext nicht übernehmen; siehe aktuelle EU-Verordnung.

states.name: Bayern
states.instrument: Handlungsleitfaden KI in der pädagogischen Praxis | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: KI als schulisches Betriebsmittel vor Einsatz durch die Schulleitung freigeben lassen. Personenbezogene Eingaben in frei verfügbare Chatbots vermeiden; bei zugelassenen Systemen Rechtsgrundlage, AV-Vertrag und Zweckbindung prüfen. Der Leitfaden verlangt Ausschluss eigener Trainingszwecke und Übermittlungen in Staaten außerhalb des DSGVO-Geltungsbereichs. Die Lehrkraft bleibt für Bewertung verantwortlich.
states.limits: Die territoriale Aussage stammt aus dem Leitfaden, nicht aus einem generellen DSGVO-Verbot aller Nicht-EU-Anbieter.

states.name: Berlin
states.instrument: Empfehlungen zum Umgang mit KI-Anwendungen am Beispiel ChatGPT | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Leistungsbewertung muss die individuell zurechenbare Eigenleistung erfassen. Bei freiwilliger Nutzung eines Lehrkraftzugangs im Unterricht dürfen keine personenbezogenen Daten Lernender eingegeben werden. Angeordnete private Schülerkonten sind mit freiwilliger Einwilligung nicht zu rechtfertigen. Formatives KI-Feedback ist von schulischer Leistungsbewertung zu unterscheiden.
states.limits: Technische Aussagen zu damaligen ChatGPT-Konten nicht als aktuelle Produkteigenschaften verwenden.

states.name: Brandenburg
states.instrument: Handlungsleitfaden zur Nutzung textgenerierender KI-Systeme | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Der Leitfaden behandelt Eigenleistung, Transparenz über KI-Nutzung und die Grenzen von KI-Detektoren. Datenschutz und Urheberrecht bleiben beim Einsatz im Unterricht einzuhalten; personenbezogene Lernendendaten gehören nicht in frei verfügbare KI-Anwendungen. Lehrkräfte müssen Ergebnisse sachlich prüfen. Die Handreichung erlaubt keine eigenständige verbindliche Notenentscheidung durch KI.
states.limits: Pädagogische Empfehlung; keine eigenständige gesetzliche Erlaubnis für externe KI-Korrektur.

states.name: Bremen
states.instrument: KI-Handreichung für Schulen | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: KI darf die Bewertung unterstützend vorbereiten; die Lehrkraft trägt die nicht delegierbare Verantwortung. Bei solchen Verfahren sind der KI-Einsatz schon bei Aufgabenstellung transparent zu machen, datenschutzkonforme Werkzeuge zu verwenden und keine personenbezogenen Daten weiterzugeben. Eine Empfehlung der KI ersetzt die eigene pädagogische Beurteilung nicht.
states.limits: Gilt im beschriebenen schulischen Kontext; keine allgemeine Freigabe beliebiger Anbieter.

states.name: Hamburg
states.instrument: LI-Leitlinien für den Einsatz von KI-Systemen | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Die Schulleitung verantwortet den schulischen Datenschutz. Bei freiwilliger Plenumsnutzung eines Lehrkraftzugangs dürfen keine personenbezogenen Schülerdaten übertragen werden. Private Schülerkonten ohne datenschutzkonforme Lösung sollen nicht angeordnet werden. Leistungsanforderungen und Regeln zur Offenlegung der KI-Nutzung müssen klar sein; die Hinweise betreffen vor allem Lernendenarbeit, nicht eine Zulassung autonomer KI-Benotung.

states.name: Hessen
states.instrument: Künstliche Intelligenz in Schule und Unterricht | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: KI kann nicht personenbezogenes formatives Feedback unterstützen. Personenbezogene Schülerdaten dürfen nicht in die beschriebenen frei verfügbaren Anwendungen eingegeben werden; Lernende dürfen nicht zu unzulässiger Nutzung verpflichtet werden. Bewertbar bleibt die individuell erbrachte Leistung nach den bestehenden schulrechtlichen Regeln.
states.limits: Die Beispiele zur Lernunterstützung sind keine allgemeine Erlaubnis für summative KI-Benotung.

states.name: Mecklenburg-Vorpommern
states.instrument: Handreichung zum Einsatz von KI an Schulen | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Formative Rückmeldungen und technische Bewertungsbeispiele werden beschrieben. Datenschutzrechtlich verlangt die Handreichung, keine personenbezogenen Daten über Prompts oder Klasseninformationen an die KI zu senden; bei personenbezogener Verarbeitung sind Rechtsgrundlage, erforderlicher AV-Vertrag und DSFA vorab zu prüfen. Beispiele ersetzen keine schulrechtliche Erlaubnis verbindlicher KI-Noten.
states.limits: Historische Lizenzangebote im PDF sind keine aktuelle Anbieterfreigabe.

states.name: Niedersachsen
states.instrument: Hinweise zum Umgang mit KI | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Die Schulleitung verantwortet die schulische Nutzung. Der Bildungsserver nennt AV-Verträge und den Ausschluss von Trainingsnutzung; personenbezogene Daten dürfen nicht in Chatbot-Prompts oder hochgeladene Dokumente eingegeben werden. Erforderliche Kompetenzmaßnahmen sollen dokumentiert werden. Die Hinweise ergänzen die Freigabe- und Datenschutzregeln des § 31 NSchG.
states.limits: Die Kompetenzdarstellung ist mit dem seit 2026 geänderten Art. 4 KI-VO abzugleichen.
states.locator: Hinweise zu Datenschutz, Verantwortung und KI-Kompetenz

states.name: Nordrhein-Westfalen
states.instrument: Medienberatung NRW: Fragen zur KI-Nutzung im Bereich Schule | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Die FAQ beschreibt KI-Nutzung ohne personenbezogene Daten. Pseudonymisierung genügt nicht automatisch; Originaldaten dürfen nicht erst zur Anonymisierung an einen ungeprüften KI-Dienst gehen. Ergebnisse sind durch Lehrkräfte zu prüfen; private Schülerkonten dürfen nicht unzulässig erzwungen werden. Die FAQ ist zusammen mit SchulG, VO-DV I, dem MSB-Leitfaden 2023 und dem differenzierteren LDI-Bericht 2026 zu lesen.
states.limits: Die Quellen unterscheiden sich im Zuschnitt: FAQ-Vorsichtsaussage und mögliche gesetzlich abgesicherte Verarbeitung im LDI-Bericht nicht gleichsetzen.

states.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
states.instrument: Schule.Medien.Recht., Baustein 5.10: KI und rechtliche Herausforderungen | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Der Baustein nennt § 67 SchulG als mögliche Grundlage bei notwendiger schulischer Verarbeitung, fordert aber für die beschriebenen KI-Eingaben den Verzicht auf personenbezogene Daten. Trainingsnutzung ist zu deaktivieren. Ergebnisse müssen geprüft werden; die letzte Entscheidung soll bei Menschen bleiben. Lehrkräfte sollen Lernende und Eltern über zulässige Nutzung informieren.
states.limits: Der Webtext setzt Hochrisiko teilweise fälschlich mit Verbot gleich und nennt alte EU-Fristen. Diese Aussagen werden ausdrücklich nicht übernommen.

states.name: Saarland
states.instrument: Online-Schule Saarland: AIS.chat, Einführung und FAQ | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Die amtliche Seite enthält konkrete Hinweise für AIS.chat: Ein Grundlagenkurs ist Zugangsvoraussetzung, schulische Gremien sollen beteiligt und Lernende angeleitet werden. Die Seite beschreibt den Ausschluss von Modelltraining sowie EU-Speicherung für diesen Dienst. Das sind dienst- und plattformspezifische Aussagen; sie belegen keine Freigabe für Gradias oder jedes andere KI-System.
states.limits: Eigenständige allgemeine landesweite Handreichung zur KI-Benotung in dieser Recherche nicht gefunden. Plattformhinweise vorhanden; kein Beweis, dass sonstige Regeln fehlen.

states.name: Sachsen
states.instrument: Wissenschaftliches Arbeiten unter Berücksichtigung generativer KI | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Schulformspezifische LaSuB-Empfehlung für Fach-/Belegarbeiten: KI-Hilfsmittel ausdrücklich zulassen; Eigenleistung und Nutzung dokumentieren. Keine personenbezogenen Eingaben; vertraglich kontrollierte Zugänge und kein Modelltraining. Fehler im KI-Feedback vor Einbeziehung in die Bewertung korrigieren. Keine allgemeine Freigabe autonomer KI-Benotung.
states.limits: API-Zugang allein schafft keine Anonymität. Die Aussage zu § 44a UrhG ersetzt nicht die Prüfung, ob dessen enge Voraussetzungen tatsächlich erfüllt sind.

states.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
states.instrument: LISA: Komplexe Leistungen in Zeiten generativer künstlicher Intelligenz | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: LISA bestätigt die Handreichung für Sekundarstufe I und II. Bei nicht beaufsichtigten komplexen Leistungen soll KI-Nutzung pädagogisch begleitet werden. Maßgeblich sind die Gestaltung der Aufgabe und die Beurteilung eigenständiger Leistung. Die Veröffentlichung behandelt vor allem KI als Lernendenhilfsmittel; daraus folgt keine Freigabe eines KI-Systems als selbstständiger Prüfer.
states.limits: Veröffentlichung und Geltungszuschnitt amtlich bestätigt; der DOI-Volltext war beim Abruf nicht zuverlässig erreichbar. Keine weiteren Detailpflichten aus nicht gelesenem Volltext codiert.

states.name: Schleswig-Holstein
states.instrument: KI@Schule – Handreichung zum Umgang mit KI | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Die veröffentlichte Handreichung lehnt die Bewertung von Schülerarbeiten durch KI ab und betont die persönlich zu erbringende Prüfungsbewertung. Sie verweist auf § 16 Abs. 2 SchulG, § 13 Abs. 4 GemVO und §§ 19, 29 OAPVO. Die Schulleitung verantwortet den Datenschutz. Die Aussage ist enger als eine allgemeine Erlaubnis mit abschließender Lehrerunterschrift.
states.limits: Stand der gefundenen Handreichung 2023; keine behauptete allgemeine neue Erlaubnis durch spätere Änderungen von Prüfungsformaten.

states.name: Thüringen
states.instrument: Handlungsleitfaden zum Umgang mit generativen KI-Modellen | Empfehlung / amtliche Handreichung
states.finding: Der Leitfaden verlangt, personenbezogene Daten einzelner Lernender und ganzer Klassen nicht an die beschriebenen Systeme zu übermitteln. Die Schulleitung trägt Verantwortung. Nicht personenbezogene formative Rückmeldungen und sprachliche Vorkorrektur werden von der schulrechtlichen Bewertung der Eigenleistung getrennt; § 48 ThürSchulG bleibt maßgeblich.
states.limits: Keine Gleichsetzung von formativer Hilfe und verbindlicher KI-Benotung.

readme.label: How to use
readme.text: Read the row as a specific requirement. Each column is one identified instrument; parent Acts and principal implementing regulations are separated where the supplied research combined them. Hover over Yes cells and timing headers for conditions.

readme.label: Yes
readme.text: The reviewed relevant provisions, official guidance or identified regulatory conditions state that requirement. Conditions and future commencement dates remain essential. For a recommendation, Yes means recommended/expressly stated there, not independently statutory.

readme.label: No
readme.text: The requirement is not stated in the reviewed relevant provisions of that instrument. No is not permission, proof that the instrument never discusses a related topic, or a conclusion about all laws that apply to a deployment.

readme.label: Illustrative template replaced
readme.text: The original example rows have been replaced by 60 requirements derived from the actual research. Blanket consent or country/provider bans were not inferred from conditional legal duties.

readme.label: Scope
readme.text: Germany, UK and the selected US federal/state instruments supplied in the country documents, plus German state guidance. This is not a complete 50-state US survey or a review of every school/university examination order.

readme.label: Types
readme.text: National Law = domestic primary legislation; State Law = subnational primary legislation, not municipal Local Law; Regulation = delegated/domestic or supranational regulation; Recommendation = guidance. Recognition conditions and contractual standards have their own types. No international treaty or municipal ordinance was identified as a separate operative source.

readme.label: Germany
readme.text: EU GDPR and the AI Act are EU regulations, not International Law treaties. Germany’s document uses German type labels, including Bundesgesetz/Landesgesetz/Verordnung/Empfehlung. Guidance can explain existing law without itself being a new law.

readme.label: No blanket approval conclusion
readme.text: A human signature, a free trial, removal of names or EU hosting does not by itself establish lawful AI grading. Institutional authority, assessment rules, lawful data flows and the actual supplier chain must be assessed separately.

readme.label: Future / phased duties
readme.text: EU AI Act dates are phased under the 2026 amendment. California ADMT and Colorado SB26-189 duties start 1 January 2027. Oklahoma’s substantive duties and later school-policy deadline differ. Yes does not mean a future provision already applies.

readme.label: Germany states
readme.text: All 16 states have a documented official source. Saarland: platform-specific AIS.chat guidance. Sachsen-Anhalt: official publication notice verified; linked guide full text was not reliably retrievable. No unseen detailed obligations were inferred.

readme.label: Conflicting source language
readme.text: Some older guides contain old AI Act dates, confuse high-risk status with prohibition, or simplify API anonymity/copyright. The tracked Germany review identifies these points. Legislation controls over an outdated paraphrase.

readme.label: Generic contracts
readme.text: US-37 is included in the instrument register but excluded from binary coding because no executed institution-specific contract was supplied. UK awarding rules and incorporated DfE standards are explicitly labelled with their limited legal effect.

readme.label: Product evidence
readme.text: The older Gradias website drafts contain claims about school permission, roles, DPAs and human review that conflict with the later research. Actual hosting, no-training, deletion, subprocessors, certification and completed assessments require evidence; the source files do not certify those facts.

readme.label: Source filing
readme.text: Data Privacy Research / Sources / Research_2026-10-10 contains the linked HTML/CSV source register, manifest and available PDF copies. Source Archive lists all research links and input-document links; historical references are retained for provenance.

readme.label: Source verification
readme.text: The supplied country documents are the baseline. Primary sources were consulted for state guidance and material time-sensitive provisions. Links found only in older inputs are marked as historical/source links rather than claimed as newly verified authority.

readme.label: Tracked documents
readme.text: The Germany, UK, US and Questions Answers DOCX files are revised with genuine Word insertions/deletions and Track Changes enabled. Their previous versions are backed up before replacement.

readme.label: Documents reviewed
readme.text: Current four DOCX files, the pitch deck, earlier website compliance drafts and comments, existing NRW sources, historical archive versions, the empty FAQ Sheet and the two certification-vendor links.
